title: Dirichlet's Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions
description: For any two positive coprime integers a and q, there are infinitely many primes congruent to a modulo q. This foundational result in analytic number theory uses Dirichlet characters and L-functions.

overview.historicalContext:
Dirichlet's theorem (1837) was the first use of analytic methods to prove results about the distribution of primes. While Euclid had proved there are infinitely many primes (c. 300 BCE), Dirichlet showed something far more refined: primes are equidistributed among arithmetic progressions.

The proof required Dirichlet to invent entirely new mathematical machinery: Dirichlet characters (group homomorphisms from (Z/qZ)* to C*) and L-functions (infinite series generalizing the Riemann zeta function). These tools became foundational for all of analytic number theory.

The key difficulty is proving that L(1, chi) is not zero for non-principal characters chi. For real characters, this requires showing the residue at s=1 is positive, which Dirichlet accomplished through careful analysis.
overview.problemStatement:
**Dirichlet's Theorem** (1837):

For any two positive coprime integers $a$ and $q$ (i.e., $\gcd(a, q) = 1$), there are infinitely many prime numbers $p$ such that:
$$p \equiv a \pmod{q}$$

Equivalently, every arithmetic progression $a, a+q, a+2q, a+3q, \ldots$ where $\gcd(a,q) = 1$ contains infinitely many primes.

**Examples:**
- There are infinitely many primes of the form $4k+1$ (i.e., 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, ...)
- There are infinitely many primes of the form $4k+3$ (i.e., 3, 7, 11, 19, 23, ...)
- There are infinitely many primes of the form $6k+1$ (i.e., 7, 13, 19, 31, 37, ...)
overview.text:
This formalization proves Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions: for coprime a, q, there are infinitely many primes p ≡ a (mod q). The proof uses Dirichlet characters χ: (ℤ/qℤ)* → ℂ* and L-functions L(s, χ) = Σ χ(n)/n^s, with the key analytic input being the non-vanishing L(1, χ) ≠ 0 for non-principal characters (which prevents cancellation in the sum over primes).

The file axiomatizes the deep analytic components (character orthogonality, L-function non-vanishing) and derives the infinitude conclusion, the density result (primes equidistribute among residue classes), and special cases including primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) and primes ≡ 3 (mod 4). Commentary connects to the Chebotarev density theorem (the generalization to number fields), class field theory, and Linnik's theorem on the smallest prime in an arithmetic progression.
overview.proofStrategy:
Dirichlet's original proof uses analytic methods:

**1. Dirichlet Characters**
Define characters chi: (Z/qZ)* -> C* as group homomorphisms, extended to all integers by setting chi(n) = 0 when gcd(n,q) > 1.

**2. Dirichlet L-Functions**
For each character chi, define:
$$L(s, \chi) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\chi(n)}{n^s}$$

These converge for Re(s) > 1 and can be analytically continued.

**3. Orthogonality Relations**
Using character orthogonality:
$$\sum_{\chi} \chi(a)^{-1} \log L(s, \chi) = \phi(q) \sum_{p \equiv a \pmod q} \frac{1}{p^s} + O(1)$$

**4. Non-vanishing at s=1**
The key step: prove L(1, chi) is not zero for non-principal chi. As s -> 1+, the left side behaves like log(1/(s-1)), which diverges. This forces the sum over primes to diverge, proving infinitude.

**5. Mathlib Implementation**
Mathlib provides a complete formal proof chain from L-function non-vanishing to the infinitude statement.
keyInsights: Dirichlet characters are the key: multiplicative functions that 'detect' residue classes mod q
L(1, chi) != 0 for non-principal chi is the heart of the proof - this is hard for real characters
The proof gives equidistribution: primes are roughly equally distributed among the phi(q) coprime residue classes
Mathlib's proof uses modern machinery: analytic continuation, Euler products, and functional equations
The special cases (primes 1 mod 4, 3 mod 4, etc.) serve as concrete instantiations — the 3 mod 4 case even admits an elementary proof via Euclid-style argument

sections.title: Basic Definitions
sections.summary: Definitions of arithmetic progressions, coprimality, and sets of primes in progressions.
sections.mathContext: $\text{ArithmeticProgression}(a, d) := \{n \in \mathbb{N} \mid \exists k, n = a + kd\}$. $\text{PrimesCongruentMod}(a, d) := \{p \text{ prime} \mid p \equiv a \pmod{d}\}$.

sections.title: Dirichlet's Theorem - Primary Formulations
sections.summary: Multiple equivalent formulations: ZMod, natural number congruence, constructive, integer, and filter-theoretic versions.
sections.mathContext: ZMod form: $\text{Set.Infinite}\{p \text{ prime} \mid (p : \mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z}) = a\}$ for $a \in (\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^*$. Constructive form: $\forall n, \exists p > n, p \text{ prime} \wedge p \equiv a \pmod{q}$.

sections.title: Dirichlet Characters and L-Functions

sections.title: Special Cases
sections.summary: Concrete applications: infinitely many primes congruent to 1 or 3 mod 4, and 1 or 5 mod 6.
sections.mathContext: Four instances: $\{p \equiv 1 \pmod 4\}$, $\{p \equiv 3 \pmod 4\}$, $\{p \equiv 1 \pmod 6\}$, $\{p \equiv 5 \pmod 6\}$ are each infinite. Each proved via `dirichlet_modEq` with coprimality by `decide`.

sections.title: Connections to Other Results
sections.summary: Relations to the Prime Number Theorem for arithmetic progressions and Linnik's theorem.
sections.mathContext: PNT for APs: $\pi(x; q, a) \sim x / (\phi(q) \ln x)$. Linnik: $\exists L, \forall a, q, \gcd(a,q)=1 \implies \min\{p \equiv a \pmod q\} \leq q^L$. Best known $L \leq 5$.

crossReferences.description: Sophie Germain primes > 3 satisfy p ≡ 5 (mod 6); Dirichlet's theorem guarantees infinitely many primes in this residue class
Dirichlet's theorem vastly generalizes Euclid's infinitude of primes by proving infinitude within each coprime residue class
Sophie Germain's work on FLT relied on primes in specific residue classes; Dirichlet's theorem guarantees their abundance
The Chinese Remainder Theorem decomposes Z/qZ into prime-power components, paralleling how Dirichlet characters factor

PNT ($\pi(x) \sim x/\ln x$) is the quantitative refinement of the infinitude of primes. Dirichlet's theorem is the equidistribution refinement: primes are not only infinite but spread uniformly across coprime residue classes. PNT for arithmetic progressions ($\pi(x; q, a) \sim x/(\varphi(q) \ln x)$) combines both, proved via Dirichlet L-functions

Both are foundational results in algebraic number theory. Dirichlet's theorem uses characters mod $q$ to detect primes in residue classes; quadratic reciprocity determines when $p$ is a quadratic residue mod $q$. The quadratic (Legendre) symbol $\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ is the simplest Dirichlet character, and $L(1, \chi_{\text{quad}}) \neq 0$ is the key non-vanishing result

Zhang's bounded prime gaps proof requires the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem, which is a mean-value estimate for the error term in Dirichlet's theorem applied to many moduli simultaneously. Dirichlet's theorem guarantees primes in each residue class; Bombieri-Vinogradov quantifies how uniformly distributed they are on average

Euler's proof that $\sum 1/p$ diverges was the prototype for Dirichlet's method: Dirichlet showed $\sum_{p \equiv a \pmod{q}} 1/p$ diverges for each coprime $a$, using L-functions to separate the contribution of each residue class via character orthogonality

Kronecker-Weber (every abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is contained in a cyclotomic field) provides the class field theory framework that generalizes Dirichlet's theorem. Dirichlet characters are the Galois-theoretic data of cyclotomic extensions, and the splitting of primes in these extensions is governed by Artin reciprocity

Hilbert's 9th problem asks for the most general reciprocity law in algebraic number fields. Dirichlet's theorem is the first major application of reciprocity to prime distribution: the non-vanishing $L(1, \chi) \neq 0$ for non-principal characters is equivalent to certain reciprocity statements, and Artin reciprocity generalizes this to arbitrary abelian extensions

conclusion.summary:
This formalization captures one of the most important theorems in analytic number theory. Dirichlet's 1837 proof was revolutionary: it introduced L-functions and character theory, techniques that would later be essential for the Prime Number Theorem (1896) and remain central to modern number theory.

Mathlib provides a complete formal proof, building on:
- Dirichlet character theory in `Mathlib.NumberTheory.DirichletCharacter`
- L-function construction in `Mathlib.NumberTheory.LSeries.DirichletContinuation`
- Non-vanishing results in `Mathlib.NumberTheory.LSeries.Nonvanishing`
- The infinitude statement in `Mathlib.NumberTheory.LSeries.PrimesInAP`
conclusion.implications:
**Consequences and Generalizations:**

**1. Prime Number Theorem for Arithmetic Progressions**
Not only are there infinitely many primes p = a (mod q), but the count up to x is asymptotically x/(phi(q) * ln(x)).

**2. Linnik's Theorem (1944)**
The smallest prime p = a (mod q) satisfies p <= q^L for some absolute constant L (currently known: L <= 5).

**3. Chebotarev Density Theorem**
Generalizes Dirichlet to number fields: primes split according to Galois conjugacy classes with density |C|/|G|.

**4. Langlands Program**
L-functions are central to the Langlands program, a vast generalization connecting representation theory, number theory, and geometry.
openQuestions: Siegel zeros: Can L(1, chi) be very close to 0 for real characters? This affects the error term in PNT for arithmetic progressions.
Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions: All non-trivial zeros have real part 1/2.
Effective bounds: What is the best constant in Linnik's theorem? Conjecturally L = 2.
